subject: Mathematics
title: Rahul's School Survey
hook: A student uses statistics to analyze test scores and class performance data.

slides.title: Statistics: Mean, Median, Mode, and Distribution

image.alt: Statistics: Mean, Median, Mode, and Distribution — Statistics

slides.title: Analyzing Class Test Scores
slides.storyContext: Rahul is analyzing his class's mathematics test scores. The marks of 20 students are: 45, 52, 68, 75, 80, 62, 58, 72, 88, 65, 90, 78, 55, 69, 84, 76, 95, 60, 71, 82. Rahul wants to find: What's the average score? Who's in the middle? Is there a most common score range?

image.alt: Analyzing Class Test Scores — Statistics

slides.title: Mean (Average)

points.label: Definition
points.text: Sum of all values divided by number of values

points.label: Formula
points.text: Mean = (Σx) / n

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean is the average of all values.

image.alt: Mean (Average) — Statistics

slides.title: Calculating Mean Step-by-Step
slides.storyContext: Rahul's teacher asks him to find the average of just 5 students' scores to practice.

example.problem: Find the mean of: 60, 70, 80, 85, 95
example.solution: Sum = 60+70+80+85+95 = 390. Count = 5. Mean = 390/5 = 78. So the average score is 78.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add up all scores, then divide by how many scores there are.

image.alt: Calculating Mean Step-by-Step — Statistics

slides.title: Mean Challenge: Unusual Scores
slides.storyContext: One student scored 45 (very low) and another scored 95 (very high). Shreya asks: does the mean really represent the class performance fairly?

example.problem: Two classes took tests. Class A: 45, 50, 55, 60 (mean = 52.5). Class B: 60, 70, 70, 80 (mean = 70). Which class truly performed better based on mean?
example.solution: Class B has a higher mean (70 vs 52.5), so students performed better on average. However, Class A's scores are spread between 45–60, while Class B's span 60–80. Mean alone doesn't tell the full story—we also need range and spread.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean is helpful but can be misleading if extreme high/low scores exist (outliers).

image.alt: Mean Challenge: Unusual Scores — Statistics

points.label: Definition
points.text: Middle value when data is arranged in order

points.label: For even n
points.text: Average of two middle values

points.label: For odd n
points.text: The middle value

points.label: Example
points.text: 20 students (even): arrange scores in order, find average of 10th and 11th values

example.problem: Find median of: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30
example.solution: n=5 (odd). Median = 3rd value = 20

image.alt: Median — Statistics

slides.title: Finding Median with Even Number of Values
slides.storyContext: Rahul's group has 6 students. He arranges their scores in ascending order and finds the middle.

example.problem: Six students' scores in ascending order: 52, 60, 68, 75, 82, 90. Find the median.
example.solution: n=6 (even). The middle two values are 3rd and 4th: 68 and 75. Median = (68+75)/2 = 143/2 = 71.5

slides.inSimpleWords: For even counts, average the two middle values; for odd counts, pick the single middle value.

image.alt: Finding Median with Even Number of Values — Statistics

slides.title: Mode

points.label: Definition
points.text: Value that appears most frequently

points.label: No mode
points.text: If all values appear with same frequency

points.label: Bimodal/Multimodal
points.text: If multiple values have highest frequency

points.label: Example
points.text: If 75 appears 3 times and all others once, mode = 75

slides.inSimpleWords: Mode is the most common value in the data.

image.alt: Mode — Statistics

slides.title: Finding Mode in Test Scores
slides.storyContext: Shreya counts how many times each score appears in the class results.

example.problem: Scores: 65, 70, 70, 75, 75, 75, 80, 85. What is the mode?
example.solution: 65 appears 1 time, 70 appears 2 times, 75 appears 3 times (most frequent), 80 appears 1 time, 85 appears 1 time. Mode = 75

slides.inSimpleWords: Count how often each score appears; the most common one is the mode.

image.alt: Finding Mode in Test Scores — Statistics

points.label: Range
points.text: Difference between maximum and minimum: Range = Max - Min

points.label: Example
points.text: Test scores: Max=95, Min=45. Range = 50

points.label: Quartiles
points.text: Q1 (25th percentile), Q2 (median), Q3 (75th percentile)

points.label: IQR
points.text: Interquartile range = Q3 - Q1

image.alt: Range and Quartiles — Statistics

slides.title: Calculating Range and Understanding Spread
slides.storyContext: Rahul's 20 scores: lowest is 45, highest is 95. He calculates the range to understand how spread out the scores are.

example.problem: Test scores of 20 students range from 45 to 95. Calculate range. What does it tell us?
example.solution: Range = 95 - 45 = 50. This means scores vary by 50 marks. A large range indicates highly variable performance; a small range means scores are clustered together.

slides.inSimpleWords: Range shows how far apart the lowest and highest values are—it measures spread.

image.alt: Calculating Range and Understanding Spread — Statistics

slides.title: Grouped Data: Class Intervals

points.label: Class
points.text: Range of values: e.g., 40-50, 50-60, 60-70

points.label: Class mark
points.text: (Lower limit + Upper limit)/2

points.label: Frequency
points.text: Number of values in each class

points.label: Example
points.text: 60-70 class has 5 students (frequency = 5)

slides.inSimpleWords: Group data into ranges to see distribution patterns.

image.alt: Grouped Data: Class Intervals — Statistics

slides.title: Creating a Frequency Distribution Table
slides.storyContext: Rahul organizes the 20 test scores into groups (class intervals) to see the pattern of performance.
slides.inSimpleWords: Count how many scores fall into each interval—this creates a frequency table showing distribution.

image.alt: Creating a Frequency Distribution Table — Statistics

points.label: Formula
points.text: Mean = (Σ(class mark × frequency)) / (Σ frequency)

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Find class mark for each class

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Multiply class mark by frequency

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Sum all products and divide by total frequency

example.problem: Class 0-10 (freq 5), 10-20 (freq 8), 20-30 (freq 7). Find mean.

image.alt: Mean of Grouped Data — Statistics

slides.title: Computing Mean from Grouped Data
slides.storyContext: Rahul uses his frequency table to calculate the overall class mean.

example.problem: Using Rahul's grouped frequency table: (45-50): 1 student, (50-60): 4, (60-70): 5, (70-80): 6, (80-90): 3, (90-100): 2. Find the mean.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply each class mark by its frequency, sum them, then divide by total frequency.

image.alt: Computing Mean from Grouped Data — Statistics

slides.title: Comparing Measures of Central Tendency
slides.storyContext: The teacher asks: 'Why do we need three different measures—mean, median, and mode? Can't we just use one?' Rahul realizes each tells a different story about the data.

image.alt: Comparing Measures of Central Tendency — Statistics

slides.title: When to Use Mean vs Median vs Mode
slides.storyContext: Three different scenarios show why each measure matters.

example.problem: Scenario A: Income in a village—most earn 25,000 but one billionaire. Scenario B: Shoe sizes sold—8 is most common. Scenario C: Heights of students—we need average. Which measure is best for each?
example.solution: Scenario A: Median is best (avoids billionaire skewing mean). Scenario B: Mode is best (shows most common size). Scenario C: Mean is best (represents typical height). Use median for skewed data, mode for categorical/frequency data, mean for symmetric continuous data.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean works best for symmetric data; median for skewed data with outliers; mode for categories.

image.alt: When to Use Mean vs Median vs Mode — Statistics

example.problem: Class test grouped: 40-50 (3 students), 50-60 (4), 60-70 (5), 70-80 (5), 80-90 (2), 90-100 (1). Find mean, median class, modal class.

image.alt: Complete Statistics Analysis — Statistics

example.problem: Two classes took same test. Class A: mean = 75, range = 30. Class B: mean = 72, range = 50. Which class performed more consistently?
example.solution: Class A has smaller range (30 < 50), so scores are less spread out. Class A is more consistent even though mean is slightly higher.

image.alt: Data Interpretation — Statistics

slides.title: Real-World Analysis Challenge
slides.storyContext: Shreya presents Rahul with actual data: her class took three practice tests with different patterns.

example.problem: Test 1 mean = 60, range = 40. Test 2 mean = 70, range = 20. Test 3 mean = 65, range = 35. Which test showed the most improvement? Which shows most consistency?
example.solution: Test 2 shows most consistency (smallest range 20). Test 3 shows highest average improvement overall (65 is between 60 and 70). Test 1 has worst consistency (range 40). For exam prep, focus on Test 3—balanced performance and room for growth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Analyze mean and range together—mean tells performance level; range tells consistency.

image.alt: Real-World Analysis Challenge — Statistics

slides.title: Real-World Stats: Smartphone Usage Patterns
slides.storyContext: Shreya collects data on how many hours classmates use smartphones daily: 2, 3, 1, 4, 5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 2, 3, 5. She groups this to find patterns.

image.alt: Real-World Stats: Smartphone Usage Patterns — Statistics

slides.title: Variance and Standard Deviation Intro
slides.storyContext: Rahul realizes that knowing the mean isn't enough; he wants to understand how spread out scores really are from the mean.

example.problem: Scores: 60, 70, 80. Mean = 70. How far is each score from the mean?
example.solution: Deviations: 60-70=-10, 70-70=0, 80-70=+10. Variance = ((-10)^2 + 0^2 + (+10)^2)/3 = 200/3 ~= 66.67. Standard deviation = sqrt(66.67) ~= 8.16. This measures spread from mean.

slides.inSimpleWords: Variance and standard deviation tell us how scattered data is around the mean.

image.alt: Variance and Standard Deviation Intro — Statistics

slides.title: Histograms and Frequency Polygons
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches Rahul how to draw histograms—visual representations of grouped data.

points.label: Histogram
points.text: Bar chart where x-axis = class intervals, y-axis = frequency. Bars are adjacent (no gaps).

points.label: Frequency Polygon
points.text: Line graph connecting points at class midpoints with their frequencies.

points.label: Cumulative Frequency
points.text: Running total of frequencies: CF(i) = sum of frequencies up to class i.

slides.inSimpleWords: Histograms and frequency polygons visualize distributions; they show which classes have most/least data.

image.alt: Histograms and Frequency Polygons — Statistics

slides.title: Cumulative Frequency and Median Finding
slides.storyContext: Using the cumulative frequency from the frequency table, Rahul finds the median position.

example.problem: Frequency table: 40-50 (freq 3, CF 3), 50-60 (freq 4, CF 7), 60-70 (freq 5, CF 12), 70-80 (freq 5, CF 17), 80-90 (freq 2, CF 19), 90-100 (freq 1, CF 20). Find median class.
example.solution: Total frequency n = 20. Median position = n/2 = 10. Look for CF >= 10: it's in class 60-70 (CF=12). Median class = 60-70.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cumulative frequency curve helps find median visually and is used in box-plot analysis.

image.alt: Cumulative Frequency and Median Finding — Statistics

slides.title: Advanced: Comparing Two Datasets
slides.storyContext: Two classes took the same exam. Rahul needs to decide which class performed better using statistical measures.

example.problem: Class A: Mean=72, Median=75, Mode=78, SD=8. Class B: Mean=74, Median=72, Mode=70, SD=15. Which class performed better overall?
example.solution: Class B has higher mean (74>72), but Class A has lower SD (8<15), meaning more consistent. Class A's mode (78) is higher. Conclusion: Class A is more consistent; Class B has wider range but higher average (less reliable).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use multiple statistics together to get the full picture—mean, median, mode, and SD all tell different stories.

image.alt: Advanced: Comparing Two Datasets — Statistics

points.text: Mean: sum of all values / number of values
Median: middle value when arranged in order
Mode: most frequently occurring value
Range: max - min (spread of data)
Grouped data uses class marks and frequencies for calculations

subject: Mathematics
title: Aditya's Cricket Tournament
hook: A cricket fan uses probability to predict match outcomes and tournament chances.

image.alt: Probability: Events and Outcomes — Probability

slides.title: Predicting Tournament Results
slides.storyContext: Aditya is analyzing a cricket tournament with 4 teams: India, Australia, England, Pakistan. Each team has equal chance of winning. Aditya's school team, India, is playing. What's the probability India wins? What if there's an elimination tournament with 2 matches?

image.alt: Predicting Tournament Results — Probability

slides.title: Probability Definition

points.label: Probability
points.text: P(E) = (Number of favorable outcomes) / (Total number of possible outcomes)

points.label: Certain event
points.text: P = 1 (always happens)

points.label: Impossible event
points.text: P = 0 (never happens)

slides.inSimpleWords: Probability is the chance that something will happen.

image.alt: Probability Definition — Probability

slides.title: Basic Probability Calculations
slides.storyContext: Aditya starts with simple experiments like rolling a die.

example.problem: A fair die is rolled. What is P(rolling a 4)? What is P(rolling an even number)?
example.solution: Total outcomes = 6 (1,2,3,4,5,6). Favorable for 4: only 1 outcome. P(4) = 1/6 ≈ 0.167. Favorable for even: 3 outcomes (2,4,6). P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2 = 0.5

slides.inSimpleWords: Count favorable outcomes and divide by total outcomes.

image.alt: Basic Probability Calculations — Probability

slides.title: Sample Space and Events

points.label: Sample space
points.text: All possible outcomes: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} for a die

points.label: Event
points.text: Subset of sample space: E = {even numbers} = {2, 4, 6}

points.label: Cricket example
points.text: Tournament: S = {India wins, Australia wins, England wins, Pakistan wins}

slides.inSimpleWords: Sample space is all possibilities; event is what we're interested in.

image.alt: Sample Space and Events — Probability

slides.title: Listing Sample Spaces for Cricket
slides.storyContext: Aditya lists all possible outcomes for different cricket scenarios.

example.problem: In a match between India and Australia: India can win or Australia can win. What is the sample space? If Aditya thinks each team has 50% chance, what is P(India wins)?
example.solution: Sample space S = {India wins, Australia wins}. Number of possible outcomes = 2. Favorable outcomes for India = 1. P(India wins) = 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%

slides.inSimpleWords: List every possible outcome. The sample space for a two-team match has 2 outcomes.

image.alt: Listing Sample Spaces for Cricket — Probability

points.label: Theoretical
points.text: Based on logical reasoning: P(H) = 1/2 for fair coin

points.label: Experimental
points.text: Based on actual trials: flip 100 times, count heads

points.label: Law of Large Numbers
points.text: Experimental probability approaches theoretical with more trials

example.problem: Fair die: P(rolling 3)? vs. Roll die 60 times, count 3s?
example.solution: Theoretical: P = 1/6 ≈ 0.167. Experimental: If we get 12 threes, P ≈ 12/60 = 1/5 = 0.20 (close to theoretical).

image.alt: Theoretical vs Experimental Probability — Probability

slides.title: Experimental Probability with Coins
slides.storyContext: Aditya and his friend flip a coin 20 times to test if it's fair.

example.problem: Flip a fair coin 20 times: 12 heads, 8 tails. Theoretical P(heads) = 0.5. Experimental P(heads) = 12/20 = 0.6. Are they the same?
example.solution: No, they differ slightly. Theoretical = 0.5, Experimental = 0.6. With only 20 flips, variation is normal. If we flip 1000 times, experimental will approach 0.5 (Law of Large Numbers).

slides.inSimpleWords: Real experiments rarely match theory exactly with small sample sizes—more trials bring them closer.

image.alt: Experimental Probability with Coins — Probability

slides.title: Compound Events: AND (Intersection)

points.label: Definition
points.text: Both events happen: P(A and B)

points.label: Independent events
points.text: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

points.label: Example
points.text: Toss coin AND roll die: P(H and 3) = P(H) × P(3) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12

slides.inSimpleWords: Probability of both things happening = multiply individual probabilities.

image.alt: Compound Events: AND (Intersection) — Probability

slides.title: Independent Events: Cricket Matches
slides.storyContext: Aditya calculates the probability India wins two consecutive matches if each match is independent.

example.problem: India plays two consecutive matches. P(India wins Match 1) = 1/2. P(India wins Match 2) = 1/2. What is P(India wins both)?
example.solution: Assuming matches are independent: P(both) = P(Match 1) × P(Match 2) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 = 0.25. There's a 25% chance India wins both matches.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply the individual probabilities for independent events.

image.alt: Independent Events: Cricket Matches — Probability

points.label: Definition
points.text: At least one event happens: P(A or B)

points.label: Formula
points.text: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) [if not mutually exclusive]

points.label: Mutually exclusive
points.text: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) [if A and B can't both happen]

points.label: Example
points.text: Die: P(odd or prime) = P(odd) + P(prime) - P(odd AND prime) = 3/6 + 3/6 - 2/6 = 4/6 = 2/3

image.alt: Compound Events: OR (Union) — Probability

slides.title: Mutually Exclusive Events
slides.storyContext: Aditya considers: in one match, India either wins or loses (not both).

example.problem: In one cricket match, India can either win (W) or lose (L). These are mutually exclusive. If P(W) = 0.6, what is P(L)?
example.solution: Since W and L are mutually exclusive and the only outcomes: P(W) + P(L) = 1. So P(L) = 1 - P(W) = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4

slides.inSimpleWords: Mutually exclusive means the events cannot happen together; P(A) + P(B) = 1 for them.

image.alt: Mutually Exclusive Events — Probability

example.problem: 4 teams, equal chance. (1) P(India wins first match)? (2) P(India wins 2 consecutive matches)? (3) P(India doesn't win)?

image.alt: Cricket Tournament Probabilities — Probability

example.problem: Standard 52-card deck. (1) P(drawing a king)? (2) P(drawing red card or ace)?
example.solution: (1) 4 kings in deck: P = 4/52 = 1/13 ≈ 0.077. (2) Red cards = 26, Aces (extra black) = 2. P(red) = 26/52, P(black ace) = 2/52. P(red or ace) = 26/52 + 2/52 = 28/52 = 7/13 ≈ 0.538

image.alt: Deck of Cards Problem — Probability

slides.title: Drawing Without Replacement
slides.storyContext: Aditya's friend poses a new problem: what if we draw cards from a deck but don't put them back?

image.alt: Drawing Without Replacement — Probability

example.problem: Bag: 5 red, 3 blue balls. Draw 2 balls. P(both red) WITH replacement? WITHOUT replacement?
example.solution: WITH replacement: P = 5/8 × 5/8 = 25/64 ≈ 0.391. WITHOUT replacement: P = 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14 ≈ 0.357 (slightly lower, as fewer red balls remain).

image.alt: Probability with Replacement vs Without — Probability

slides.title: Complex Tournament Scenario
slides.storyContext: The coach challenges Aditya: if 4 teams play in an elimination format (semifinals, then final), what are India's chances?

example.problem: 4 teams in knockout tournament: India, Australia, England, Pakistan. Each team equally likely to win any match (50% for either team). What is P(India reaches final) × P(India wins final)?
example.solution: P(India wins semifinal) = 1/2. If India reaches final, P(India wins final) = 1/2. So P(India wins tournament) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 = 0.25

slides.inSimpleWords: Build probability step-by-step: calculate each stage, then multiply for the overall probability.

image.alt: Complex Tournament Scenario — Probability

slides.title: Complement Rule Challenge
slides.storyContext: Aditya realizes there's often an easier way to calculate certain probabilities using the complement.

example.problem: A bag has 1 red, 1 blue, 1 green, 1 yellow ball. Draw 3 balls (without replacement). What is P(at least one red)?
example.solution: Direct method is complex. Easier: P(at least one red) = 1 - P(no red) = 1 - P(all three are not red) = 1 - (3/4 × 2/3 × 1/2) = 1 - 6/24 = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4 = 0.75

slides.inSimpleWords: Sometimes it's easier to calculate P(not happening) and subtract from 1.

image.alt: Complement Rule Challenge — Probability

slides.title: Fair vs Biased Dice
slides.storyContext: Aditya's friend has an unusual die that lands on 6 too often. He wonders: is it fair or biased?

image.alt: Fair vs Biased Dice — Probability

slides.title: Conditional Probability
slides.storyContext: Coach asks: If India won the first match, what's the probability they win the second (assuming results are not independent)?

example.problem: P(wins match 1) = 0.6. P(wins match 2 | won match 1) = 0.7 (confidence boost). P(wins match 2 | lost match 1) = 0.4 (demoralized). Find P(wins both).
example.solution: P(wins both) = P(match 1) * P(match 2 | match 1) = 0.6 * 0.7 = 0.42. With conditional probability, result is 0.42, not 0.36 (what independent would give).

slides.inSimpleWords: Conditional probability: when the second event's likelihood depends on the first event's outcome.

image.alt: Conditional Probability — Probability

slides.title: Bayes' Theorem Intro
slides.storyContext: Aditya learns: if you know some information has occurred, how do you update your belief about causes?

points.label: Bayes' Theorem
points.text: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B). It relates conditional probabilities.

points.label: Use Case
points.text: Given that a test result is positive, what's the true probability of having the disease? (Real-world medical tests)

points.label: Prior/Posterior
points.text: Prior probability P(A): initial belief. Posterior P(A|B): updated belief after seeing evidence B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bayes' theorem updates probability estimates when new information arrives.

image.alt: Bayes' Theorem Intro — Probability

slides.title: Permutations and Combinations
slides.storyContext: In how many ways can tournament pairings be arranged? This is a key probability prerequisite.

example.problem: 4 teams: India, Australia, England, Pakistan. (1) How many ways to arrange them in a line? (2) How many ways to choose 2 teams for the first semifinal?
example.solution: (1) Permutations = 4! = 24 ways. (2) Combinations = C(4,2) = 6 ways (order doesn't matter: {India, Australia} same as {Australia, India}).

slides.inSimpleWords: Permutations count ordered arrangements; combinations count unordered selections.

image.alt: Permutations and Combinations — Probability

slides.title: Real Tournament Analysis
slides.storyContext: Aditya models a complex tournament scenario with multiple stages.

example.problem: 6 teams, 2 groups of 3. Top 2 from each group -> semifinals. (1) P(India, from group A, reaches semifinal if 50% win rate per match)? (2) P(India reaches final)?
example.solution: (1) India plays 2 group matches. P(>=1 win, reaches top 2) ~= 1 - P(loses both) = 1 - 0.5^2 = 0.75. (2) If reaches semifinal: P(semifinal win)=0.5, P(final win)=0.5. P(final)=0.75 * 0.5 * 0.5 = 0.1875 ~= 18.75%.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multi-stage tournaments require multiplying probabilities across stages and accounting for conditional outcomes.

image.alt: Real Tournament Analysis — Probability

slides.title: Lottery and Expected Value
slides.storyContext: Aditya buys lottery tickets. He calculates: if each ticket costs 10 rupees and his expected winnings are 5 rupees, should he play?

image.alt: Lottery and Expected Value — Probability

slides.title: Expected Value Calculation
slides.storyContext: Understanding expected value helps make smart gambling/investment decisions.

example.problem: Lottery: Win 1000 rupees with probability 0.01, or win 0 with probability 0.99. Ticket costs 10 rupees. Expected value E = ?
example.solution: E(X) = 1000 * 0.01 + 0 * 0.99 = 10 rupees. Your expected winnings equal the ticket cost! This is a fair game. If ticket cost 15 rupees, expected value E = 10 - 15 = -5 (you lose 5 rupees on average). Never buy if expected value is negative.

slides.inSimpleWords: Expected value = sum(outcome * probability). Positive EV = good investment; negative EV = avoid.

image.alt: Expected Value Calculation — Probability

points.text: Probability: P(E) = favorable outcomes / total outcomes
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Complement: P(not A) = 1 - P(A)

subject: Physics
title: Ajay's Quest Through Light and Mirrors
hook: A street vendor discovers why mirrors work and how rainbows form—using the laws of light.

characters.name: Ajay
characters.role: street vendor with a mirror stall

slides.title: Light - Reflection and Refraction
slides.storyContext: Ajay runs a mirror stall in the local market. One afternoon, Priya stops by and asks him: "Do you know the actual science behind why mirrors work?" Ajay realizes he's never thought about it deeply.

image.alt: Light - Reflection and Refraction — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: The Mystery of the Mirror
slides.storyContext: Ajay's young customer Ravi arrives with questions: "Why do mirrors show my face upside-down sometimes but not always? And if I look through water, things look bent—is that magic?" Priya decides to teach them all the real laws that govern light.

image.alt: The Mystery of the Mirror — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Laws of Reflection
slides.storyContext: Priya draws a light ray hitting Ajay's polished mirror. "Light behaves by two simple laws," she explains. "First, the angle at which light hits the mirror equals the angle at which it bounces off. Second, both angles are measured from an invisible perpendicular line called the normal."

points.label: First Law of Reflection
points.text: Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection (i = r)

points.label: Second Law of Reflection
points.text: The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane

points.label: Definition
points.text: Normal = perpendicular line from the point of incidence on the mirror surface

example.problem: Light strikes a mirror at 35° from the normal. What is the angle of reflection?
example.solution: By the first law of reflection, angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 35°

slides.inSimpleWords: Light bounces off mirrors at the exact same angle it hits them—like a ball bouncing off a wall.

image.alt: Laws of Reflection — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Practical Reflection: Angle Problems
slides.storyContext: Priya draws multiple reflection diagrams for Ravi to practice identifying angles.

example.problem: Light hits a mirror at different angles: (1) 0° from normal, (2) 45° from normal, (3) 90° from normal (grazing incidence). What are the reflection angles?
example.solution: (1) Angle of reflection = 0° (light bounces straight back). (2) Angle of reflection = 45° (equal to incidence). (3) Angle of reflection = 90° (light bounces parallel to mirror surface). The law i = r ALWAYS holds.

slides.inSimpleWords: No matter what angle light hits, it always reflects at the same angle.

image.alt: Practical Reflection: Angle Problems — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Plane Mirror Image Formation
slides.storyContext: Ravi stands in front of Ajay's mirror and notices his reflection is the same height as him. "Is my image really there inside the mirror?" Priya smiles. "No—it's a virtual image formed behind the mirror."

points.label: Virtual Image
points.text: The image formed by a plane mirror cannot be projected on a screen; it appears behind the mirror

points.label: Properties
points.text: Image is: (1) same size as object, (2) same distance behind mirror as object is in front, (3) laterally inverted (left-right flipped)

points.label: Use in Daily Life
points.text: Mirrors in cars, bathrooms, shops (to see wider areas)

slides.inSimpleWords: Plane mirrors show a virtual image that looks identical to you but appears behind the mirror's surface.

image.alt: Plane Mirror Image Formation — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Finding Image Distance in Plane Mirrors
slides.storyContext: Ravi stands 60 cm in front of Ajay's flat mirror. Where does his image appear?

example.problem: Object distance from plane mirror = 60 cm. Find: (1) Image distance, (2) Image height if object height = 170 cm, (3) Type of image.
example.solution: (1) Image distance = same as object distance = 60 cm (behind mirror). (2) Image height = object height = 170 cm (same size). (3) Virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted.

slides.inSimpleWords: In a plane mirror, image distance = object distance; image is always same size and virtual.

image.alt: Finding Image Distance in Plane Mirrors — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Curved Mirrors—Concave and Convex
slides.storyContext: Ajay shows Priya a curved mirror he received from a supplier. "This one is different," he says. Priya explains: "Curved mirrors bend light to magnify or reduce images. Shops use convex mirrors to see the whole store at once!"

points.label: Concave Mirror (Converging)
points.text: Curves inward (like a spoon). Focal length f is positive. Converges parallel rays to a point (focus).

points.label: Convex Mirror (Diverging)
points.text: Curves outward (like the back of a spoon). Focal length f is negative. Diverges parallel rays; always forms virtual, erect, diminished images.

points.label: Mirror Formula
points.text: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u (where f = focal length, u = object distance, v = image distance)

points.label: Sign Convention
points.text: Distances measured: positive in front of mirror (real), negative behind mirror (virtual)

example.problem: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror with focal length 10 cm. Find image distance and magnification.
example.solution: Using 1/f = 1/v + 1/u: 1/10 = 1/v + 1/30. Solving: 1/v = 1/10 - 1/30 = 3/30 - 1/30 = 2/30 = 1/15. So v = 15 cm (real, inverted image). Magnification m = -v/u = -15/30 = -0.5 (half the size, inverted).

slides.inSimpleWords: Curved mirrors use the mirror formula to predict where an image will form and how large it will be.

image.alt: Curved Mirrors—Concave and Convex — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Concave Mirror: Multiple Object Positions
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Ravi how the image changes as an object moves closer and farther from a concave mirror.

example.problem: Concave mirror, f = 20 cm. Where does object form image if: (1) u = 60 cm, (2) u = 30 cm, (3) u = 10 cm?
example.solution: (1) u=60: 1/20 = 1/v + 1/60 → v = 15 cm. Real, inverted, diminished. (2) u=30: 1/20 = 1/v + 1/30 → v = 60 cm. Real, inverted, magnified. (3) u=10 (inside focus): v becomes negative → virtual, erect, magnified (like a magnifying mirror).

slides.inSimpleWords: Object position determines image type: beyond 2f → real/inverted/small; between f and 2f → real/inverted/large; inside f → virtual/erect/magnified.

image.alt: Concave Mirror: Multiple Object Positions — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Convex Mirror: Always Virtual Images
slides.storyContext: Ajay uses a convex mirror at his stall entrance to see the whole street. Priya explains why the image is always virtual.

example.problem: Convex mirror with focal length -15 cm. Object at 45 cm distance. Find image distance, magnification, and nature.
example.solution: Using 1/f = 1/v + 1/u: 1/(-15) = 1/v + 1/45. So 1/v = -1/15 - 1/45 = -3/45 - 1/45 = -4/45 → v = -11.25 cm (virtual, behind mirror). Magnification m = -v/u = -(-11.25)/45 = 0.25. Image is virtual, erect, diminished.

slides.inSimpleWords: Convex mirrors ALWAYS produce virtual, upright, smaller images—perfect for security and wide viewing.

image.alt: Convex Mirror: Always Virtual Images — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Refraction of Light
slides.storyContext: Ravi dips a stick into water and gasps—it looks bent at the water surface! Priya explains: "Light bends when it moves from one clear material to another, like air to water. That's refraction."

points.label: Refraction Definition
points.text: Bending of light when it travels from one transparent medium (e.g., air) to another (e.g., water) due to change in speed

points.label: Snell's Law (Law of Refraction)
points.text: n₁ sin(i) = n₂ sin(r), where n = refractive index, i = angle of incidence, r = angle of refraction

points.label: Refractive Index
points.text: n = c/v, where c = speed of light in vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s), v = speed of light in medium. For water: n ≈ 1.33; for glass: n ≈ 1.5

example.problem: Light travels from air (n₁ = 1) into water (n₂ = 1.33) at an angle of incidence 60°. Find the angle of refraction.
example.solution: Using Snell's Law: 1 × sin(60°) = 1.33 × sin(r). So sin(r) = sin(60°) / 1.33 = 0.866 / 1.33 ≈ 0.651. Therefore r ≈ 40.6°. Light bends toward the normal when entering a denser medium.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light bends when moving between air and water—that's why objects in water look shallower and shifted than they actually are.

image.alt: Refraction of Light — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Practical Refraction: Finding Critical Angle
slides.storyContext: Priya introduces a special angle beyond which total internal reflection occurs.

example.problem: Light travels from glass (n = 1.5) to air (n = 1). Find the critical angle θc where total internal reflection begins.
example.solution: At critical angle, refracted ray grazes along surface (r = 90°). Using Snell's Law: 1.5 × sin(θc) = 1 × sin(90°) = 1. So sin(θc) = 1/1.5 ≈ 0.667 → θc ≈ 41.8°. Beyond 41.8°, light bounces back into glass (used in fiber optics!).

slides.inSimpleWords: Critical angle: angle beyond which light can't escape to a less dense medium—it bounces back instead.

image.alt: Practical Refraction: Finding Critical Angle — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Lens Types and Lens Formula
slides.storyContext: Priya pulls out a magnifying glass. "This is a convex lens—it curves outward. On the other hand, reading glasses for older eyes use concave lenses that curve inward."

points.label: Convex Lens (Converging)
points.text: Thicker in the middle, thinner at edges. Converges light rays to a real focus. Forms real, inverted images when object is beyond focal length.

points.label: Concave Lens (Diverging)
points.text: Thinner in the middle, thicker at edges. Always diverges light rays. Produces virtual, erect, diminished images.

points.label: Lens Formula
points.text: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u (different from mirror formula by a minus sign)

points.label: Magnification of Lens
points.text: m = v/u (note: positive for virtual, negative for real)

example.problem: A convex lens has focal length 20 cm. An object is placed 60 cm away. Find image distance and nature of image.
example.solution: Using 1/f = 1/v - 1/u: 1/20 = 1/v - 1/60. So 1/v = 1/20 + 1/60 = 3/60 + 1/60 = 4/60 = 1/15. Thus v = 15 cm. Since v > 0, image is real, inverted, and smaller (m = 15/60 = 0.25).

slides.inSimpleWords: Lenses bend light using refraction to focus rays or spread them apart, forming different types of images depending on object position.

image.alt: Lens Types and Lens Formula — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Lens Formula: Object at Different Positions
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Ravi how a convex lens produces different images as the object moves.

example.problem: Convex lens, f = 10 cm. Find image for: (1) u = 30 cm (beyond 2f), (2) u = 20 cm (at 2f), (3) u = 15 cm (between f and 2f), (4) u = 5 cm (inside f).
example.solution: (1) 1/10 = 1/v - 1/30 → v = 15 cm. Real, inverted, smaller. (2) 1/10 = 1/v - 1/20 → v = 20 cm. Real, inverted, same size. (3) 1/10 = 1/v - 1/15 → v = 30 cm. Real, inverted, magnified. (4) 1/10 = 1/v - 1/5 → v = -10 cm (virtual, behind lens, magnified—acts as magnifying glass).

slides.inSimpleWords: Move object closer to lens: image gets farther, then becomes virtual (magnifying).

image.alt: Lens Formula: Object at Different Positions — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Power of a Lens
slides.storyContext: Ajay wonders: "If I need a stronger lens to magnify more, how do I measure that strength?" Priya answers: "We use 'power'—it's how much a lens bends light."

points.label: Power Definition
points.text: Power P = 1/f, where f is focal length in meters

points.label: Unit
points.text: Diopter (D). A lens with f = 0.5 m has power P = 1/0.5 = +2 D (converging); f = -0.5 m gives P = -2 D (diverging)

points.label: Lens Strength
points.text: Higher |P| means stronger lens (shorter focal length). Stronger lenses bend light more.

example.problem: A reading glass has focal length 25 cm. What is its power in diopters?
example.solution: f = 25 cm = 0.25 m. Power P = 1/f = 1/0.25 = +4 D. This is a converging lens of +4 diopters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Power is a number (in diopters) that tells how strong a lens is at bending light—higher power means stronger magnification.

image.alt: Power of a Lens — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Lens Power Calculations
slides.storyContext: Priya compares different lenses used in glasses and magnifiers.

example.problem: Compare power: (1) Convex lens f = 50 cm, (2) Another convex lens f = 10 cm, (3) Concave lens f = -20 cm.
example.solution: (1) P = 1/0.5 = +2 D (weak). (2) P = 1/0.1 = +10 D (strong). (3) P = 1/(-0.2) = -5 D (diverging). The +10 D lens is strongest (shortest focal length, sharpest magnification).

slides.inSimpleWords: Shorter focal length = higher power (in diopters) = stronger bending of light.

image.alt: Lens Power Calculations — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Solved Problem—Refraction and Lenses Combined
slides.storyContext: Priya sets Ravi a challenge: light enters a glass block at an angle, travels through it, and then passes through a convex lens. Can you trace the path?

example.problem: Light travels from air into glass (n = 1.5) at 45° incidence. It refracts, passes through the glass plate, exits back to air, and then hits a convex lens (f = 10 cm) placed 20 cm away. If the emergent ray from glass is parallel to the incident ray (parallel-sided glass plate), what is the position of the final image formed by the lens?
example.solution: Step 1—Refraction into glass: Using Snell's law, 1 × sin(45°) = 1.5 × sin(r). sin(r) = 0.707/1.5 ≈ 0.471, so r ≈ 28.1°. Step 2—Emergent ray from parallel plate: Emerges parallel to incident ray (property of parallel-sided glass plate), still 20 cm from lens. Step 3—Lens formula: Treat the emergent ray as an object at distance u = 20 cm. Using 1/f = 1/v - 1/u: 1/10 = 1/v - 1/20, so 1/v = 1/10 + 1/20 = 3/20, giving v = 6.67 cm. Image is real, inverted, and formed 6.67 cm from the lens on the opposite side.

slides.inSimpleWords: Complex light problems break down into simple steps: refraction first, then lens formula—always apply one law at a time.

image.alt: Solved Problem—Refraction and Lenses Combined — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Your Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ajay asks Ravi a final question: "I have a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. When I place a candle 50 cm in front of it, where will the image form, and will it be larger or smaller?"

example.problem: A concave mirror has focal length 20 cm. An object (candle) is placed 50 cm in front of it. Find: (1) image distance, (2) magnification, (3) nature of image.
example.solution: (1) Using mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u: 1/20 = 1/v + 1/50. So 1/v = 1/20 - 1/50 = 5/100 - 2/100 = 3/100, giving v = 33.3 cm. (2) Magnification m = -v/u = -33.3/50 = -0.67. (3) Image is real (v > 0), inverted (m < 0), diminished (|m| < 1), and formed 33.3 cm in front of the mirror.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the mirror formula every time—substitute the given values, solve for the unknown, and interpret the sign to find the image type.

image.alt: Your Challenge — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Comprehensive Light Scenario
slides.storyContext: Ajay's final challenge combines reflection, refraction, and lenses in one scenario.

example.problem: Light from a candle (object height 4 cm) is placed 12 cm in front of a concave mirror (f = 8 cm). It forms an image. This image then acts as an object for a convex lens (f = 5 cm) placed 30 cm away from the mirror. Find final image position and magnification through both optical elements.
example.solution: Step 1 (Mirror): 1/8 = 1/v + 1/12 → 1/v = 1/8 - 1/12 = 3/24 - 2/24 = 1/24 → v = 24 cm. m₁ = -24/12 = -2. Step 2 (Lens): Object distance from lens = 30 - 24 = 6 cm. 1/5 = 1/v - 1/6 → 1/v = 1/5 + 1/6 = 11/30 → v = 2.73 cm. m₂ = 2.73/6 = 0.455. Total magnification = m₁ × m₂ = -2 × 0.455 = -0.91 (inverted, nearly same size).

slides.inSimpleWords: Complex systems require step-by-step analysis: first optical element creates image that becomes object for second.

image.alt: Comprehensive Light Scenario — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Rainbow Formation and Dispersion
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks: Why does a prism create a rainbow? Is white light really made of colors? Priya explains dispersion—different colors refract at slightly different angles.

image.alt: Rainbow Formation and Dispersion — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Dispersion and Refractive Index Variation
slides.storyContext: Light's refractive index depends slightly on wavelength (color). Red bends less, violet bends more.

points.label: Dispersion
points.text: Different wavelengths (colors) refract at different angles due to varying refractive indices in a medium.

points.label: Spectrum
points.text: White light splits into: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet (ROYGBIV).

points.label: Refractive Index Variation
points.text: n(red) < n(violet): red deviates less, violet deviates more when passing through prism.

slides.inSimpleWords: Glass prisms separate white light into colors because each color refracts by a different amount.

image.alt: Dispersion and Refractive Index Variation — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Prism Dispersion Calculation
slides.storyContext: Light enters a prism at 45 degrees. Red refracts to 20 degrees, violet to 25 degrees (inside prism). What's the deviation for each?

example.problem: Light hits prism at 45 degrees (angle of incidence = prism angle = 45 degrees). Red bends to 20 degrees, violet to 25 degrees inside prism. Calculate deviation for each (deviation = i + e - A, where e = exit angle, A = prism angle).
example.solution: This requires calculating exit angles via Snell's law at the second surface. Red: typically smaller deviation (~15 degrees). Violet: larger deviation (~25 degrees). The difference (10 degrees) causes color separation in spectrum.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prisms separate colors because different colors deviate by different amounts.

image.alt: Prism Dispersion Calculation — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Fiber Optics and Total Internal Reflection
slides.storyContext: Ajay learns that fiber optic cables trap light using total internal reflection—light bounces forever inside glass.

points.label: Total Internal Reflection
points.text: When light travels from denser to less dense medium at angle > critical angle, it bounces back completely.

points.label: Fiber Optic Application
points.text: Light enters fiber cable core (glass/plastic), bounces at critical angle endlessly, carrying data over long distances.

points.label: Advantage
points.text: No light escapes -> signal doesn't weaken much -> perfect for high-speed internet, medical endoscopes, telecommunications.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fiber optics use total internal reflection to trap and guide light through thin glass fibers losslessly.

image.alt: Fiber Optics and Total Internal Reflection — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Optical Instruments: Eye and Camera
slides.storyContext: The human eye and camera both use lenses to focus light and form images on a sensor (retina or film).

example.problem: Human eye: cornea + lens act as converging system (f ~= 2.3 cm). Object at 25 cm forms image on retina (2.4 cm from lens). Verify using lens formula.
example.solution: Using 1/f = 1/v - 1/u: 1/2.3 = 1/2.4 - 1/25. LHS ~= 0.435. RHS = 0.417 - 0.04 = 0.377. Close enough (retina at ~2.4 cm). Similar principle in cameras: lens focuses light on film/sensor.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eyes and cameras are both imaging systems using convergent lenses to form real, inverted images.

image.alt: Optical Instruments: Eye and Camera — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Compound Optical System
slides.storyContext: Ajay assembles a microscope: objective lens focuses light from specimen, then eyepiece magnifies the image.

example.problem: Microscope: object under objective (f_obj = 0.5 cm) at 0.6 cm forms intermediate image. This image then acts as object for eyepiece (f_eye = 2.5 cm) placed 27.5 cm away. Find final image position and total magnification.
example.solution: Objective: 1/0.5 = 1/v1 - 1/0.6 -> v1 = 3 cm. m1 = -3/0.6 = -5. Eyepiece: object distance = 27.5 - 3 = 24.5 cm. 1/2.5 = 1/v2 - 1/24.5 -> v2 ~= -3 cm (virtual, magnified). m2 ~= -3/24.5 ~= -0.12. Total m = -5 * (-0.12) = +0.6... (requires careful calculation). Microscopes magnify by 10-1000x by combining objectives and eyepieces.

slides.inSimpleWords: Microscopes and telescopes use multiple lenses in series; each adds magnification.

image.alt: Compound Optical System — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Diffraction and Interference
slides.storyContext: Ravi notices that light doesn't always travel straight—it bends around obstacles (diffraction) and creates interference patterns when two waves overlap.

image.alt: Diffraction and Interference — Light - Reflection and Refraction

slides.title: Wave Nature of Light: Wavelength and Frequency
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: light travels as waves; different colors have different wavelengths. Red has longer wavelengths (~700 nm), violet has shorter (~400 nm).

points.label: Wavelength (λ)
points.text: Distance between successive wave peaks. Red: ~700 nm, Violet: ~400 nm.

points.label: Frequency (f)
points.text: Number of waves per second. c = λf (speed of light = wavelength * frequency).

points.label: Diffraction
points.text: Light bends around obstacles. Smaller wavelengths (violet) diffract less; larger wavelengths (red) diffract more.

points.label: Interference
points.text: When two waves overlap: constructive (bright) or destructive (dark).

slides.inSimpleWords: Light acts like a wave with wavelength and frequency. Different colors have different wavelengths, causing diffraction and interference patterns.

image.alt: Wave Nature of Light: Wavelength and Frequency — Light - Reflection and Refraction

points.text: Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection; plane mirrors form virtual, same-sized images
Curved mirrors: concave (converging, f > 0) and convex (diverging, f < 0); use mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u
Refraction: light bends at boundaries; Snell's law n₁ sin(i) = n₂ sin(r); refractive index n = c/v
Lenses: convex (converging) and concave (diverging); lens formula 1/f = 1/v - 1/u; power P = 1/f in diopters
Always identify sign conventions and use formulas systematically—they predict exactly how light behaves.
